paras: The threatened lynching of Thomas C. Early took place at Leadville, Colorado, on March 28, 1882, when a crowd sought to lynch the lawyer after he shot and killed Officer Samuel Townsend. Officers hurried Early to jail under a strong guard, and the wire reported that the attempt to lynch him was frustrated. None of the reports gives the race of anyone involved.

Early was a young Leadville lawyer of the firm of Danford & Early and an active Democrat, who had moved there about three years earlier from Sedalia, Missouri. Townsend, about forty, was the constable of Judge Talbot's court and had served on the city police and as a deputy sheriff. According to a Leadville account reprinted in Sedalia, the two quarreled over fees in a replevin suit in which Early represented one party, Early claiming Townsend had overcharged him by ten or fifteen cents.

Early was accused of firing three shots at Townsend in the hallway of the Union block on Harrison avenue, wounding him fatally in the abdomen. The wire said Early forced the quarrel and that Townsend was unarmed and tried to get away, while a witness reported that Townsend's gun had not been drawn. Detective John Byrne arrested Early at the scene as a dense crowd filled the street.

The Sedalia weekly bazoo reported that Early was hurried to jail and placed under a strong guard to protect him from a mob that had gathered and threatened to lynch him. The same paper wrote that friends of the dead officer "would surely have resorted to violence if permitted," and the wire stated simply that an attempt to lynch Early was frustrated.

A Denver Republican dispatch reprinted in Sedalia said the coroner's jury recommended that Early be held for the grand jury without bail, finding the shooting "deliberate and unprovoked." The same dispatch said the excitement continued and feeling against Early was "very bitter." No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story spread as a short Leadville wire dispatch, printed on March 29 and 30 in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "From Politics to the Gallows," the Salt Lake Herald as "A Murderous Attorney," and the Carson City Morning Appeal as "Police Officer Killed." In each version the lynching attempt was a closing line after the account of the killing, and a weekly news digest a week later repeated it under "Murderous Deeds," spelling the name "Earley."

Only the Sedalia weekly bazoo, writing about a former townsman, gave fuller coverage, reprinting a long Leadville narrative under "COLD BLOOD MURDER" and a biographical item headed "A FORMER SEDALIAN." That paper treated the mob as an expression of public anger at Early and described his rescue "with difficulty," without comment on the lynching threat itself.

The wire printed the accused's name as J. C. Early, while the Sedalia paper, which knew him, called him Thomas C. Early. The wire dated the shooting to the evening of Tuesday, March 28, and the Leadville narrative to shortly before 3 that afternoon, but one Sedalia item said Monday.

bases: The wire said an attempt to lynch the accused was frustrated and the Sedalia paper said a mob threatened to lynch him before he was jailed under guard (A1, A5); no one was killed by the crowd and no race is given for anyone.

A crowd sought to lynch Early in retaliation for the killing of an officer, but the attempt was frustrated and he was held in jail (A1, A5, A7); no one was killed, so the standard definition is not met.

The Associated wire (A1) and the separately sourced Sedalia report (A5) both describe a lynching threat against Early after the shooting, though they differ on whether it was an 'attempt' or a threat.

framing.detail: Western and Midwestern dailies ran the brief wire under headlines such as 'From Politics to the Gallows', 'A Murderous Attorney' and 'Police Officer Killed', ending with the frustrated lynching.

The Sedalia weekly bazoo reported the mob threat matter-of-factly, noting the friends of the 'murdered man' would have used violence 'if permitted', while condemning Early's act as 'COLD BLOOD MURDER'.

conflicts.note: The Sedalia paper knew him as a former resident and prints the full name; the wire's 'J. C.' is likely a garble. No text seen prints 'Farley'.
